To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cultural variants linked more closely to alienable traits are adopted more readily than those linked to more inalienable traits, and that this effect can occur even when the two traits have similar practical implications.

“In our experiment, participants from one alien species were more likely to adopt cultural variants associated with the other species when they were told that those variants were associated with a more alienable trait than with an inalienable trait.”

1) cultural variants are more likely to spread between antagonistic groups if they are linked to alienable traits, 2) this effect is stronger if the alienable trait is more alienable, 3) this effect is independent of whether the alienable trait actually exists in the group, and 4) this effect can occur even in cases where the inalienable and alienable traits are associated with the same group.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spread of cultural traits between antagonistic groups, in which the traits are associated with alien species, alienable or inalienable traits.
the spread of cultural traits between antagonistic groups, and with the role of alienability in this process.
the spread of cultural traits between antagonistic groups and with the role of social bias in this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results suggest that the cultural traits of the Burls, which were associated with the more alien species and alienable trait of toughness, were more likely to be acquired by the Wiwos than those of the Burls associated with the less alien species and alien trait of Blackness.
the spread of cultural traits is not simply a matter of the traits themselves, but also depends on the traits’ associations with other, alienable traits.
the spread of cultural traits is influenced by a variety of factors, and that the relative importance of these factors may be context-dependent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
alien species and alienable features are not necessarily mutually exclusive.
the spread of a cultural variant may be promoted by its association with an alienable trait, but impeded by its association with a non-alienable one.

the spread of cultural traits may be promoted by the dissociation of traits from inalienable ones and by the association of traits with alienable ones, and that this may occur in spite of the existence of strong bias against individuals exhibiting those alienable traits.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cultural variants adopted by individuals are influenced by the degree to which the traits associated with them are alienable.
inalienable traits can act as barriers to the spread of cultural traits between groups.
inalienable traits may be a powerful force in the transmission of culture.
